catalog_quote: El acento prosódico popoloca, a diferencia del español, se manifiesta por la prolongación de la vocal de la penúltima sílaba de la palabra o de una de las consonantes de la última sílaba, sin afectar la intensidad ni el tono de ésta. La acentuación de la gran mayoría de las palabras se puede predecir, y el número de excepciones es mínimo. 0.3.1. El acento vocálico. En algunas palabras se acentúa la vocal de la penúltima sílaba. La vocal acentuada tiene una duración prolongada. Si la última sílaba de la raíz empieza con vocal o con y o v, la vocal de la penúltima sílaba siempre es prolongada. ... Si la última sílaba de una palabra que tiene el acento vocálico comienza con consonante, la prolongación de la vocal de la penúltima sílaba es importante (tiene valor fonológico), porque difiere de la duración corta de la vocal ante una consonante alargada. ... 0.3.2. sweep_summary: Only one stress-titled item exists for sanj1285: Kalstrom & Pike 1968 (Phonetica 18:16-30), already in our bibliography and already the catalog's secondary source. It is about word stress in this language. We hold only pp. 19-26 (Rosetta Project scan; copied to with). this search of works with stress in the title re-read those pages against the page image: they describe two stress types realised as consonant length (type-one) or vowel length (type-two), and p. 26 shows root stress being dropped in favour of stress-bearing suffixes (-n·a 'my', -n·ci 'little', -ʔ·ya neg.), which confirms the catalog's 'morphological' coding drawn from the 1995 Gramatica sec. 0.3-0.3.3. The missing section 1 'Stress' (pp. 16-18, the formal placement statement) and pp. 27-30 could not be obtained: Unpaywall, OpenAlex and Semantic Scholar all report the DOI (10.1159/000258596) closed with no repository copy; the De Gruyter Brill landing page returned an empty 202 and Karger a 403; HathiTrust holds Phonetica v.18-19 search-only; SIL archive entry 3726 (live) is a record only; archive.org has no other Popoloca phonology item; Google Books returned nothing; web.archive. Priority medium for the complete article (same analysts as the 1995 grammar; unlikely to change the classification). No new source supersedes the catalog's deciding source.

new_statements.reading: Stress in Atzingo Popoloca is realised as length (type-one: a lengthened syllable-initial consonant; type-two: a lengthened vowel), and a root's stress is removed when a stress-bearing suffix such as -n·a 'my', -n·ci 'little' or the negative -ʔ·ya is attached, the suffix taking the stress. This is the same accent shift to tonic suffixes that the 1995 Gramatica (sec. 0.3.3) states, so it confirms the catalog's 'morphological' coding. It is not new: the excerpt was already held and cited as the catalog's secondary source; the article's own placement statement (sec. 1, pp. 16-18) remains unread and no open copy of it exists.

sources.locator: PARTIAL copy: Rosetta Project scan pp. 19-26 only (8 pp.); quote from p. 26 (PDF p. 8), section (5) 'Syllable'; supporting lines p. 21 (sec. 2.2), p. 23 (sec. 3.2), p. 25 (sec. 4.2). Sec. 1 'Stress' (pp. 16-18) and pp. 27-30 are not in any open copy found.
sources.note: The held pages describe two stress types: type-one = lengthening of a syllable-initial consonant (raised dot after the consonant, e.g. i²⁴n·ta⁴ 'water'; p. 23 sec. 3.2 'unless the /n/ has been lengthened due to stress type-one (see 1.1)'), type-two = lengthening of the vowel (raised dot after the vowel, e.g. nta·³si³ 'market'; p. 25 sec. 4.2). Stress is realised by length, not pitch: tone is described separately and is contrastive on stressed /n/ (p. 20-21).
